title: CSRF, SameSite and Fetch Metadata
summary: Another site makes your user's browser send a request with their cookie. See how SameSite defaults help and where they do not, and defend with antiforgery tokens, Sec-Fetch-Site checks and explicit cookie flags.

steps.title: A request the user never meant
body: The user is signed in to `shop.example`. They open a page on `evil.example`, which contains:
```html
<form action="https://shop.example/account/email" method="post">
<input name="email" value="attacker@evil.example">
</form>
<script>document.forms[0].submit()</script>
```text
POST /account/email HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example
Origin: https://evil.example                     <- the browser says where it came from
Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site                       <- and how it relates to the target
Cookie: sid=<the user's session>                 <- ...but may still attach the cookie
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
email=attacker%40evil.example

If the cookie is attached, the shop sees a valid session and changes the email. A password reset later, the account is the attacker's. That is **cross-site request forgery** (CSRF). The attacker never sees the answer; they only need the side effect.

steps.prompt: The forged form posts to the shop from `evil.example`. What does the attacker's page learn from the shop's answer?
options: Nothing: the same-origin policy stops it reading the response, but the request and its side effect still happen
The full response, because the browser sent the cookie
Nothing, and the request is never sent
steps.explain: CSRF is a write-only attack. That is why antiforgery tokens work: a secret on the shop's own page is exactly what the attacker cannot read.

steps.title: SameSite: what the browser does with your cookie
body: | `SameSite=` | Sent on cross-site requests? |
| `Strict` | never (even following a link from another site: the user arrives signed out) |
| `Lax` | only on **top-level GET navigations** (clicking a link); not on cross-site POST, fetch, iframes or images |
| `None; Secure` | always (needed for real cross-site uses: embedded widgets, some SSO flows) |

Chrome and Edge treat a cookie **without** a `SameSite` attribute as `Lax` (with a short exception: for two minutes after it is set, top-level cross-site POSTs still carry it). Firefox and Safari do not apply that default. So **always set it explicitly**.
Two gaps SameSite leaves open:
1. **State changes on GET.** Lax sends the cookie on a top-level GET, so `GET /account/email?email=...` is CSRF-able from any link. Never change state on GET.
2. **Same-site is not same-origin.** `blog.shop.example` and `shop.example` are the *same site*. A compromised or user-content subdomain can CSRF the main app with `Strict` cookies.

steps.prompt: The session cookie is `SameSite=Lax`. Is it sent with the request from `https://evil.example`'s page?
items: The user clicks a link to `https://shop.example/orders`
An auto-submitted `<form method="post">` to the shop
steps.explain: Only top-level GET navigations carry a Lax cookie across sites, which is exactly why a GET endpoint that changes state is still exploitable (the lab's task 9).

steps.title: The defences, in layers
body: 1. **Antiforgery tokens** (the synchronizer token pattern). The server puts a secret in the form; the attacker's page cannot read it, so it cannot forge the POST. Built into ASP.NET Core: MVC and Razor Pages validate automatically; minimal APIs validate `[FromForm]` endpoints after `AddAntiforgery()` + `UseAntiforgery()`, and the form gets its hidden field from `IAntiforgery.GetAndStoreTokens(ctx)`.

2. **Fetch Metadata.** Modern browsers send `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin | same-site | cross-site | none` on every request. Refusing unsafe methods unless it is `same-origin` (or `none`: the user typed the URL) stops CSRF for the whole app in one middleware. If the header is missing (old browsers, `curl`), fall back to checking `Origin`.
3. **Cookie flags.** `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict`, `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, and ideally the `__Host-` name prefix (forces `Secure`, `Path=/` and no `Domain`, so a subdomain cannot overwrite it).

4. **JSON APIs** that require `Content-Type: application/json` cannot be reached by a plain cross-site form (it would need a CORS preflight). Helpful, but do not make it the only defence: one endpoint that also accepts form posts reopens the hole.
Bearer tokens in an `Authorization` header are not sent automatically by the browser, so APIs that use only them are not CSRF-able. Cookies are what make CSRF possible.

steps.prompt: A POST arrives with `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site` and a valid session cookie. The app is `shop.example`; the request came from `reviews.shop.example`, which hosts user-generated pages. What should a strict Fetch Metadata policy do?
options: Refuse it: only same-origin (or none) may send unsafe methods, because a sibling subdomain is not the app
Allow it: same-site means the same company
Allow it if the cookie is SameSite=Strict
Redirect it to the login page
steps.explain: SameSite cookies treat the sibling as the same site, so they do not help here. `Sec-Fetch-Site` distinguishes `same-site` from `same-origin`, which is exactly the gap.

steps.title: One middleware against CSRF, and honest cookie flags
prompt: 1. `POST /login` sets the `sid` cookie with `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite=Lax` (`new CookieOptions { ... }`).
2. Add a middleware that checks every request **except** `GET`, `HEAD` and `OPTIONS`:
- if `Sec-Fetch-Site` is present, allow only `same-origin` and `none`;
- if it is absent, allow when there is no `Origin` header, or `Origin` is exactly `https://shop.example`;
- otherwise answer `403` and do not call the endpoint.
`GET /account` stays reachable from anywhere. **Run checks** sends forged and honest requests.
solution: // CSRF: unsafe methods must come from our own pages.
new CookieOptions { HttpOnly = true, Secure = true, SameSite = SameSiteMode.Lax, Path = "/" });
hints: `HttpMethods.IsGet(ctx.Request.Method)` and friends tell you whether the method is safe. Read the headers with `ctx.Request.Headers["Sec-Fetch-Site"].ToString()` and `ctx.Request.Headers.Origin.ToString()` (empty when missing).
Cookie: `new CookieOptions { HttpOnly = true, Secure = true, SameSite = SameSiteMode.Lax, Path = "/" }`.
template: {{CODE}}
static class DojoTests
static async Task<HttpResponseMessage> ChangeEmail(HttpClient http, string to, string? site, string? origin)
var msg = new HttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Post, "/account/email")
Content = new FormUrlEncodedContent(new Dictionary<string, string> { ["email"] = to }),
msg.Headers.Add("Cookie", "sid=session-for-ada");
if (site is not null) msg.Headers.Add("Sec-Fetch-Site", site);
if (origin is not null) msg.Headers.Add("Origin", origin);
return await http.SendAsync(msg);
static async Task<string?> Email(HttpClient http, string? site = null)
var msg = new HttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Get, "/account");
msg.Headers.Add("Cookie", "sid=session-for-ada");
if (site is not null) msg.Headers.Add("Sec-Fetch-Site", site);
return DojoWeb.Prop(await DojoWeb.Json(await http.SendAsync(msg)), "email");
public static async Task Run(HttpClient http)
await Dojo.TryAsync("The session cookie could be checked", async () =>
var r = await http.PostAsync("/login", null);
var cookie = r.Headers.TryGetValues("Set-Cookie", out var v) ? string.Join("; ", v) : "";
Dojo.Check("sid is HttpOnly", cookie.Contains("httponly", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase), cookie);
Dojo.Check("sid is Secure", cookie.Contains("secure", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase), cookie);
Dojo.Check("sid is SameSite=Lax", cookie.Contains("samesite=lax", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase), cookie);
await Dojo.TryAsync("Forged requests could be sent", async () =>
DojoWeb.Status("a cross-site POST is refused (403)", 403, await ChangeEmail(http, "x@evil.example", "cross-site", "https://evil.example"));
DojoWeb.Status("a same-site POST from a sibling subdomain is refused", 403, await ChangeEmail(http, "x@evil.example", "same-site", "https://reviews.shop.example"));
DojoWeb.Status("no Sec-Fetch-Site, but a foreign Origin: refused", 403, await ChangeEmail(http, "x@evil.example", null, "https://evil.example"));
Dojo.Eq("...and the email is unchanged", "ada@customer.example", await Email(http));
await Dojo.TryAsync("Honest requests could be sent", async () =>
DojoWeb.Status("the shop's own form (same-origin) works", 200, await ChangeEmail(http, "ada1@customer.example", "same-origin", "https://shop.example"));
DojoWeb.Status("an old browser with our Origin works", 200, await ChangeEmail(http, "ada2@customer.example", null, "https://shop.example"));
DojoWeb.Status("a script or curl with neither header works", 200, await ChangeEmail(http, "ada3@customer.example", null, null));
Dojo.Eq("GET /account works from another site (reading is not a state change)", "ada3@customer.example", await Email(http, "cross-site"));

steps.title: Live lab: change the staff email, then stop it
prompt: In the **vulnerable shop** lab, do **Attack: change the staff email address** (a page on your `listen` server that navigates the staff member's browser to the GET endpoint) and **Fix: POST only, antiforgery tokens, SameSite** in `Account.cs`. This time use ASP.NET Core's built-in antiforgery, the token way.
steps.explain: Token, POST-only and SameSite are three layers; the lesson's Fetch Metadata middleware would be a fourth, and covers every endpoint at once.
